OF SAINT CYRIL, ARCHBISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA: DEFENSE OF THE TWELVE CHAPTERS, AGAINST THE BISHOPS OF THE EAST.

Those who have presented their minds to the all-holy God and have chosen to speak in support of the doctrines of the truth reject the profane, empty babblings of the unholy heretics. They fix the inner and hidden eye of the heart on the divinely inspired Scripture, and once they have filled it richly with good thoughts, they rise up against those who twist what is right, and very vigorously, all but saying: "I have been very zealous for the Lord." Now Nestorius was pouring out many and various blasphemies against Christ, the Savior of us all, and was, as it were, prising up from its foundations the venerable and great mystery of the Incarnation. We knew that it is not without danger to choose silence in such matters. We advised him many times to refrain from such blasphemies, but it did no good at all, and so we have been forced to the point where we must join in the contest for the doctrines of true religion.

We selected certain chapters from his blasphemies and, to good purpose, anathematized them, or rather those who wish to hold them. In this we obeyed the blessed Paul, who says: "If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed. But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed." Yet somehow certain people have been greatly displeased by this. Either they are of the same mind and opinion as he is, or they pretend to reject his views while trying by every means to help him and to make those who wish to speak up for the Savior hated. They ought to have considered that rebuking those who teach other doctrines would have shown how genuine their love for Christ was. As it is, they have not done what was better, far from it. They have made themselves the bitter enemies of those whose zealous followers they might have been, and so have shared the crown of incorruption with them. So they attack the anathematisms as badly made. Beside each one they have set down in writing the inventions of their own minds and some senseless idle talk, and they think they will carry away those who read them and who meet their words without testing them. We therefore had to set the truth against them in turn, to beat back the accusation, and to show that our opponents are fond of mockery, not searchers after the truth. So we have placed each of the anathematisms first, then arranged beside it what they composed, and then attached our own reply. We are using, as it were, those learned in the divine Scriptures as our judges, and we ask for a right and irreproachable verdict from those who know the [?]

ANATHEMATISM 1. If anyone does not confess that Emmanuel is truly God, and therefore that the holy Virgin is Theotokos (for she gave birth in a fleshly manner to the Word of God the Father become flesh), let him be anathema.

Objection of the Easterners. Who would agree that the Word from God, having become flesh, was born in a fleshly manner? For if she gave birth in a fleshly manner, she no longer did so as a virgin. And where shall we put the words, "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you," if, according to him, the Virgin gave birth in a fleshly manner and not in a manner befitting God? And how did a star, appearing in a marvelous way, point out this birth? Magi from Persia, guided by it, arrived seeking the newborn child. When they found him, they brought gifts suited both to the one perceived by the mind and to the one who appeared to sight. And angels came down from heaven [?] the birth, mingled with the shepherds and danced, singing: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will among men." Whose signs are these?

Are they signs of a fleshly birth, or of one befitting God? Besides, if we take up the words without examining them, we shall imagine a change in the Word and a transformation into flesh. In the same way we shall also suppose that he became sin and a curse, if we pay no attention to what follows or comes before the passages, or to the usage of Scripture itself. But in fact we rightly take "the Word became flesh" to mean his dwelling in the flesh, following the meaning of the Gospels.

Defense of Cyril. The all-wise John makes plain the mystery of the economy in the flesh of the only-begotten Son of God when he writes: "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us." The blessed Fathers who once gathered at Nicaea understood this rightly. They said that the very Word who was begotten of God the Father, through whom the Father made all things, Light from Light, true God from true God, was incarnate and became man. That is, he was united to flesh having a rational soul and became man, while also remaining God. No one at all doubts that the union was brought about without change and without confusion, for the Word of God remained, as I said, what he is, even though he became flesh, since he is unchangeable by nature. What is said to be made flesh is not changed into the nature of flesh. Rather, it is understood as something else existing beside the flesh and united to it. Because they thought this, the blessed Fathers named the holy Virgin Theotokos. They believed that she gave birth to the Son incarnate and made man, through whom the Father made all things. But Nestorius, the inventor of the new blasphemies among us, fights against this belief and disparages the word Theotokos as false. He spoke as follows: "I have often asked them," he says, "'Do you say that the Godhead was born of the blessed Virgin?' At once they recoil from the phrase: 'And who,' they say, 'is so sick with blasphemy as to say that in her who bore the temple, God was created by the Spirit?' Then we add: 'What strange thing are we saying, then, when we advise you to avoid the word and come to the term that signifies the two natures in common?' At that point what is said seems blasphemous to them. Either confess plainly that the Godhead was born of the blessed Mary, or, if you shun the expression as blasphemous, why do you say these things to me while pretending not to say them?" He is driving, or rather [?] impiously forcing, those who call the Virgin Theotokos into having to confess that the nature of the Godhead, bare and by itself, became the fruit of flesh, and that the Word of God took the beginning of his existence from a woman.

We therefore wished to give full assurance that we are complete strangers to such an opinion, for we have not been so foolish as to choose to think otherwise than one ought. We said that the Virgin gave birth to the Word of God become flesh according to the Scriptures, that is, become man, and that she bore him in a fleshly manner, that is, according to the flesh. God the Father begot from himself, in a divine manner, the Son who is God. But since what is born of the flesh is flesh, the Virgin, being flesh, gave birth in a fleshly manner. To say "in a fleshly manner" does not do away with the wonder of the birth. Nor does it overturn the working of the Holy Spirit, by which he formed in the womb the one who was born. Rather, it teaches that just as God begets divinely, that is, in a manner befitting God according to his own nature, so also a human being begets humanly, or flesh in a fleshly manner. But the Word, being God by nature, came forth in a manner befitting God even though he had become flesh, that is, as would befit one who is truly God. For he alone had a mother who knew no marriage, and he kept her who bore him according to the flesh a virgin. I am amazed that they hesitate to call the holy Virgin Theotokos and yet say that he was born in a manner befitting God. An ordinary man is not born in a manner befitting God. They also say that the Magi brought gifts suited both to the one perceived by the mind and to the one who appeared, and so once again they divide the Lord Jesus Christ into two after the union. But the one perceived by the mind became visible, not by a change of nature, but by union with the visible body. Indeed the sacred Scripture says that the holy apostles became eyewitnesses and ministers of the Word. Yet how is it not entirely clear [?] that the Word from God the Father is incorporeal, intangible and invisible? But I find the holy apostles saying: "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen, which we have looked upon with our eyes, and our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life." So the gifts were suited to the one, that is, to Christ, for the same one is at once God and man. That is why at his birth there were choirs of holy angels and hosts of spirits calling him Savior and Redeemer. When the evangelist says, "The Word became flesh," they say they are afraid that, if "became" keeps its proper meaning, a change might be thought to have occurred in the divine nature of the Word. I praise their fear. But I am amazed that they reject the true and necessary meaning of the expression and say that the Word became flesh in the way he might be said to have become a curse and sin. If they had any sense, should they not have seen that, having written "became," the blessed evangelist removes every suspicion of change by immediately adding:

"and dwelt among us"? It is absurd in another way, too, to dare to say that the Word became flesh in the way he is said to have become a curse and sin. He did not in fact become a curse, nor sin. Rather, though he was righteous he was counted among the lawless, so that he might abolish sin; and he who blesses creation was called accursed, so that he might loose the curse against us and free those who believe in him from punishment. So he did not truly become a curse and sin, but he was called these things in order to loose the curse and the sin. If, then, he became flesh in this way, he has abolished the flesh, just as he abolished the curse and the sin. He neither became man nor was truly incarnate. The mystery is mere appearance, and the manner of the Incarnation turns out to lie in bare names. The hope of the resurrection is destroyed completely. Into whose death, then, have we been baptized? Where is the word of faith that we preach? For we are saved by confessing that Jesus is Lord and believing that God raised him from the dead. Is our faith, then, in one like ourselves, an ordinary man, and do we no longer worship the Word who appeared in human form for our sake? Did not the one who is free, as God, take the form of the slave? Did not he who is distinguished by the heights of the Godhead humble himself? Did not he who is in the form of the Father and equal to him lower himself to self-emptying, he who distributes good things to creation from his own fullness? Away with such ill counsel! The blessed Fathers taught us otherwise. They said that the Word from God the Father was truly incarnate and became man, without change and without confusion. But the manner of the economy is wholly beyond words. I will call their own words as witnesses to what I have said.

From Peter, martyr, bishop of Alexandria. Hence the evangelist also speaks truly when he says, "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us," that is, from the time when the angel greeted the Virgin, saying, "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you." For "the Lord is with you," spoken by Gabriel, means "God the Word is with you." It signifies that he was being born in the womb and becoming flesh, as it is written: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; and the holy one to be born will be called Son of God."

From Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria. Hence also, when the flesh was born of Mary the Theotokos, he himself is said to have been born, he who gives being to all others, so that he might transfer our birth to himself.

From the same, from the Letter to Epictetus. How did those called

Christians dare even to doubt whether the Lord who came forth from Mary is Son of God by essence and by nature, while according to the flesh he is of the seed of David and of the flesh of the holy Mary? Who, then, have become so bold as to say that the Christ who suffered and was crucified in the flesh is not Lord and Savior and God and Son of the Father? Or how can those who say that the Word came upon a holy man, as upon one of the prophets, wish to be called Christians? They say that he did not himself become man by taking his body from Mary, but that Christ is one and the Word of God is another, the Word who was Son of the Father before Mary and before the ages. Or how can those who say that the Son is one and the Word of God another be Christians?

We shall follow these opinions of the holy Fathers. If anyone teaches otherwise and thinks otherwise, he is straying from the straight and royal road. The passage set out below shows that it is not unusual for the holy Fathers to say that Christ was born "in a fleshly manner"; indeed the expression is familiar to others as well, and it is no less true for us. It runs as follows:

From Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium. If he had not been born in a fleshly manner, you would not have been born spiritually. If he had not endured the form of the slave, you would not have gained the glory of adoption.

Here too "in a fleshly manner" means "according to the flesh," just as, of course, "divinely" means "according to the Godhead."

ANATHEMATISM 3. If anyone divides the hypostases in the one Christ after the union, joining them only by a conjunction of dignity, that is, of authority or power, and not rather by a coming together in natural union, let him be anathema.

Objection of the Easterners. Once again we shall remind him of his own words and show that he speaks of two hypostases, where he says in the first tome: "So then, as far as concerns his own nature, the Word from God the Father was not sanctified by himself alone; but if anyone should think that the one born of the holy Virgin alone was anointed and sanctified, and for that reason was named God..." How, then, as if he had forgotten his own words, [?] into one hypostasis, calling the divine union natural? Who will ever accept that the divine union of the mystery of the economy is natural? If the union is natural, where is grace? Where is the divine mystery? For natures, as we have been taught, once they have been fixed by God who ordered them, are slaves to the sequence of necessity. Otherwise the matter of the economy will again follow a cycle and the sequence of nature, after the nonsense and fable of the millennium of the ill-named Apollinarius [?].

Defense of Cyril. The inspired Paul, as a steward of the mysteries of God who has Christ speaking within him, makes clear to all in what manner the only-begotten Word of God became man: "For surely he does not take hold of angels," he says, "but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham. Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in matters relating to God." We crown these words with our votes for their correctness. We follow the divinely inspired Scriptures everywhere and consider the words of those who speak of God worthy of all admiration, or rather we regard them as divine laws. So we say that the Word from God the Father took hold neither of the nature of the holy angels nor of his own nature. Rather, we believe that, as the sacred Scriptures teach, he overshadowed the holy Virgin, since he is the power of the Most High Father, and formed for himself the body from her, though through the working of the Holy Spirit. He became man and was called son of Abraham and of David. He did not barter away, because of his humanity, his being truly Son of God the Father. Rather, even though he became flesh, he remained in the nature, preeminence and glory of the Godhead, for as God he is unchangeable and beyond change. So there is one and the same Son and Lord, both before the Incarnation and after it. To divide the one into two sons and to undo the reality of the true union, by separating them into parts and setting the man apart and God apart, earns the charge of the highest impiety. But Nestorius cared little for this and dared to say in these very words: "'Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a slave.' He did not say, 'Let this mind be in you which was also in God the Word, who, being in the form of God, took the form of a slave.' Instead he took 'Christ' as a name that signifies the two natures, and so without danger he names him both as taking the form of a slave and as God, since what is said is irreproachably divided according to the twofold character of the natures." And again in another exposition he says: "'That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.' Because of the one who wears it, I revere what is worn; because of the one who is hidden, I worship what appears. God is not separated from what appears; for this reason I do not separate the honor of what is not separated. I separate the natures, but I unite the worship." And again in another exposition: "Say of the one who assumed that he is God. Add of the one assumed that he is the form of a slave. Then bring in the dignity of the conjunction: that the authority of the two is

common, that the dignity of the two is the same. While the natures remain, confess the unity of the dignity." You see him everywhere distinguishing the natures from one another, but uniting, as he says, the worship, and speaking of a common authority and of the unity of dignity alone. But what is common, if it is common, would not be one. It would surely belong to two, or to more, each considered separately and apart. Why, then, do they bring so great an accusation against the argument that rightly anathematized such things? What is wrong if we raised up the doctrines of true religion against the loathsome and utterly odious words of Nestorius and took due care for the safety of the brethren? They say that I contradict my own words, and as proof they bring forward part of the letter I wrote to the holy monks, so I thought it necessary to say what is fitting about this as well. They say that I too spoke of two hypostases, and that this is enough to prove that we too chose to say the same as those who hold exactly this view. So I must first set out the part of the letter, and afterwards I will add the arguments that show they have chosen to tell falsehoods throughout. It runs as follows: "So then, as far as concerns his own nature, the Word from God the Father was not sanctified by himself alone. But if anyone should think that the one born of the holy Virgin alone was anointed and sanctified, and for that reason was named Christ, let him come forward and say whether the anointing is enough to show that the anointed one is equal in glory and shares the throne with God, who is beyond all." For Nestorius, the inventor of the new blasphemies among us, often asserts that the Word from God was named Christ separately, and that the one born of the holy Virgin is another Christ, separately and apart. We disparage that opinion as ugly, incoherent and banished from the truth. [?] We do not assert that the Word from God the Father, considered by himself, was anointed with the oil of gladness. Nor do we assert that the one from the holy Virgin was anointed separately and by himself, as a man and as a Son other than the Word from God. Rather, we insist that all must confess one Christ, the only-begotten Word of God incarnate and made man. "For there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism." It is therefore plain to anyone used to thinking rightly that they are falsifying the meaning of what I have written and slandering the truth in this as well. In another sense, it would be blameless, and quite reasonably so, and free from all reproach, to recognize that the flesh is one thing in its own nature, other than the Word begotten of God the Father, and that the Only-begotten, in turn, is another according to the principle of his own nature. But to recognize these things is not to divide the natures after the

[?] If anyone wishes to examine the power of the mystery with the keen eye of the mind, he will see that, as I said at the beginning, the Word, being God, did not take hold of his own nature but of the seed of Abraham. The holy body from the seed of Abraham, which he took from the blessed Virgin when he came forth as man, so that he might be made like his brothers and the Only-begotten might be called Firstborn, is not of one substance with the Word born of God. Yet even if the body is of another nature than the Word from God the Father, there is still one Christ, Son, God and Lord, even though he became flesh. And it is not without harm to undo the mode of the true union by separating the hypostases into two sons, so that they part from one another and exist individually and separately, and have only a conjunction that is external, as in a ranking of honour. If we call the union natural, we mean that it is true, since the divinely inspired Scripture is accustomed to use the word in this way. For the divine Paul writes somewhere to certain people: "And we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest." Surely no one would say that the divine wrath has a natural subsistence, so that sinners are to be thought of as its offspring; otherwise we should be wholly and entirely of one mind with those who suffer from the madness of the Manichaeans. No, "by nature" means "in truth." So we do not confuse the natures, or mix them up with one another, as our opponents claim, when we say that the union came about naturally. Rather, we everywhere affirm that from two unlike realities, divinity and humanity, there came to be the one Christ, Son and Lord. As for the doctrines of Apollinarius, they are no concern of ours at all; for those long since condemned as counterfeiters of the truth must be shunned.

ANATHEMA 4. If anyone distributes between two persons, that is, hypostases, the expressions in the Gospel and apostolic writings, whether spoken about Christ by the saints or by him about himself, and attaches some of them to a man thought of separately apart from the Word from God the Father, and others, as befitting God, to the Word from God the Father alone, let him be anathema. Objection of the Easterners. Here too it is fitting to remind him of his own pronouncements, in which he says: "Even if you hear that he advanced in wisdom, stature and grace, do not suppose that the Word of God became wise by progress; nor again dare foolishly to say that we attribute advancing in stature, wisdom and grace to the man." Here he even denies the testimony of Scripture, which teaches that the progress happened to the Lord according to the nature of the visible flesh. But now is not the time [?] [?]

to refute this, since we are pressing on to the chapter before us; for we have set out what he said earlier in order to show that he speaks of two hypostases and contradicts himself. "Now, one must not apply the expressions by dividing the union, that is, the one Son, into two persons, or hypostases, or two sons; for the supreme union is indivisible and inseparable, and the one Son is one in every respect, in principle, manner and concept. But while the supreme union is safeguarded, and the one Son, Christ and Lord is confessed, what is said must be understood of one and the same Son. Yet it is fitting that what is said be applied to the one Son according to the power of the united natures." But not to distinguish [?] the expressions in the Gospels, whether those spoken by the Lord himself about himself or those found in the apostolic writings — what excess of blasphemy does that not exceed? For if we do not divide the expressions, how could we stand up to the followers of Eunomius and Arius, who jumble everything together as spoken of one nature, and blasphemously refer the lowly things of the humanity to the most exalted nature of the pure Godhead? Or how shall we understand the words of the Lord, spoken on account of the nature of the visible flesh: "I did not come to do my own will"; and "I have received a command what to say and what to speak"; and "I do nothing of myself"; and "I am going to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God"; and all the rest of this kind? If the expressions remain undivided, as the natures do, then on his view the Father will be God of the only-begotten God, and the Son, in his Godhead, will be a minister and servant of the Father's commands. And if we take the lowly things as referring to the nature of the Godhead, to whom shall we apply "I and the Father are one," and that he acts as the Father does, and "For as the Father raises the dead, so the Son also gives life" to whom he wills, and not to whom he is commanded? Rather, according to the Lord's own word, the Father is rightly both Father and God: God of the one who [?] in later times from the seed of David with flesh [?], and Father of God the Word, begotten from him impassibly and eternally, while the sonship is preserved and confessed in its single form. And how shall we understand "Truly, truly I say to you, before Abraham came to be, I am," and "All things came into being through him"? If the expressions remain undivided, shall we attach to the nature that came from the seed of David in later times the being before Abraham and David, and the coming into being of all things through it? Or shall we say, as piety requires, that while the natures remain unconfused and the union is confessed indivisible, [John 8:58]

the expressions are applied according to the power of the united natures, as was said before, to the one Son, Lord and Christ, but without gathering everything up into one nature? So that, because of the supreme union, which is beyond our comprehension, both natures are understood even from a name belonging to one of them; as, for instance, in "No one has ascended into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven," and "If then you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before": do we not, from the title "Son of Man," understand also the one joined to him without confusion and yet without separation? For even if he called himself Son of Man because of the nature of the flesh that was assumed and seen, yet through the things accomplished by him he [showed himself] God [?]. And again: "Jesus Christ, through whom are all things." And again: "Jesus Christ, the same yesterday and today and forever." If yesterday and today, how are all things through him? And if all things are through him, how is he yesterday and today? Yet "All things through him" is true, "Yesterday and today" is trustworthy, and "The same forever" is true, if we apply the expressions according to the difference of the natures united without confusion and without separation: understanding "yesterday and today" of what is seen, "forever" of what is perceived by the mind, and "one and the same" of the singleness of the sonship. Defence of Cyril. It seems, then, that those who wish rashly to criticize the anathemas we drew up so usefully and necessarily aim not to think or say anything true, but simply to make the matter a plain display of their love of fault-finding. For if they had been sober [?] and had applied their minds carefully to what is written, they would not have failed to see that by their own votes and by the arguments they have put forward they confirm the anathema rather than show that it was composed ignorantly. In what way, I will explain. Our worthy Nestorius said something like this when preaching in church: "To put it more clearly and more intelligibly for everyone: the followers of Arius, Eunomius and Apollinarius, and all the choirs of that faction, are eager to introduce 'Theotokos,' so that, a mixture having taken place and the natures not being divided, none of the lowly things may be ascribed to the humanity, and they may then have room to attack the Godhead, as though everything said were said of one." Since this is what was said, the anathema we composed was most useful, for it does not permit the one Lord Jesus Christ to be divided into two persons and hypostases. [Notes: "Aim, as" [?]; "of the things said"; "most usefully"; [?]; "about".]

And that they agree with our very words is surely clear from what they have written and resolved to hold. It runs thus: "Now, one must not apply the expressions by dividing the union, that is, the one Son, into two persons, or hypostases, or two sons; for the supreme union is indivisible and inseparable, and the one Son is one in every respect, in principle, manner and concept. But while the supreme union is safeguarded, and the one Son, Christ and Lord is confessed, what is said must be understood of one and the same Son. Yet it is fitting that what is said be applied to the one Son according to the power of the united natures." So then, if the union to the utmost degree is preserved, what entry for division, or even the notion of it, could still creep in? And how can the one who dares to divide not stray from the straight road and wholly depart from the doctrines of true religion? What, then, does the anathema say? If anyone divides the expressions in this way, attaching some to a man thought of separately apart from the Word from God, and others, as befitting God, to the Word from God alone, let him be anathema. If, then, those who separate and distinguish them, assigning some to a man individually and separately and others to God the Word individually and separately, are not dividing the one Christ and speaking of two sons, let these lovers of accusation be angry with us. But if to think this way is cutting and division, on what ground have they resolved to censure our words, when they themselves, as they say, confess that Emmanuel is undivided and one by supreme union? Now, that each expression must be understood with discernment, even if it happens to be spoken by him himself, I would commend myself, as I think would everyone accustomed to right thinking; for some are befitting God, while others are better suited to the economy in the flesh. But since he is one and the same, God and man together, for that very reason he quite rightly speaks sometimes as God and sometimes as man. Yet we insist that both kinds are the expressions of the one Jesus Christ, neither stripping the temple born of the all-holy Virgin of the Godhead, nor regarding the Word from God the Father as fleshless after the ineffable union. I am amazed that, though they are extremely meddlesome and, as they think, subtly scrutinize my letters, they deliberately pass over everything in them that is useful and necessary to prove the correctness and precision of the doctrines, but pounce eagerly on anything that has, in their opinion, even a faint ground for suspicion, so as to use it to make false accusations against us. I will recall my own words. For I wrote thus in the letter to Nestorius: "The expressions of our Saviour in the Gospels we neither [divide] between two persons [Notes: "Son" [?]; "to take hold of"; "as anyone"; "not separating"; "not two"; "of the sayings".]

to refute this, since we are pressing on to the chapter before us; for we have set out what he said earlier in order to show that he speaks of two hypostases and contradicts himself. And if we take the lowly things as referring to the nature of the Godhead, to whom shall we apply "I and the Father are one," and that he acts as the Father does, and "For as the Father raises the dead, so the Son also gives life" to whom he wills, and not to whom he is commanded? Rather, according to the Lord's own word, the Father is rightly both Father and God: God of the one who [?] in later times from the seed of David with flesh [?], and Father of God the Word, begotten from him impassibly and eternally, while the sonship is preserved and confessed in its single form. And how shall we understand "Truly, truly I say to you, before Abraham came to be, I am," and "All things came into being through him"? If the expressions remain undivided, shall we attach to the nature that came from the seed of David in later times the being before Abraham and David, and the coming into being of all things through it? Or shall we say, as piety requires, that while the natures remain unconfused and the union is [confessed] indivisible, [Notes: "nor"; [?]; "perhaps 'and the one Son'"; "and of the one Son"; "to divide"; "of the flesh of David"; "according to the flesh"; "perhaps 'again'"; "shall we attach".]

confessed indivisible, the expressions are applied according to the power of the united natures, as was said before, to the one Son, Lord and Christ, but without gathering everything up into one nature? So that, because of the supreme union, which is beyond our comprehension, both natures are understood even from a name belonging to one of them; as, for instance, in "No one has ascended into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven," and "If then you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before": do we not, from the title "Son of Man," understand also the one joined to him without confusion and yet without separation? For even if he called himself Son of Man because of the nature of the flesh that was assumed and seen, yet through the things accomplished by him he showed himself to be God. And again: "Jesus Christ, through whom are all things." And again: "Jesus Christ, the same yesterday and today and forever." If yesterday and today, how are all things through him? And if all things are through him, how is he yesterday and today? Yet "All things through him" is true, "Yesterday and today" is trustworthy, and "The same forever" is true, if we apply the expressions according to the difference of the natures united without confusion and without separation: understanding "yesterday and today" of what is seen, "forever" of what is perceived by the mind, and "one and the same" of the singleness of the sonship. Defence of Cyril. It seems, then, that those who wish rashly to criticize the anathemas we drew up so usefully and necessarily aim not to think or say anything true, but simply to make the matter a plain display of their love of fault-finding. For if they had been sober [?] and had applied their minds carefully to what is written, they would not have failed to see that by their own votes and by the arguments they have put forward they confirm the anathema rather than show that it was composed ignorantly. In what way, I will explain. Our worthy Nestorius said something like this when preaching in church: "To put it more clearly and more intelligibly for everyone: the followers of Arius, Eunomius and Apollinarius, and all the choirs of that faction, are eager to introduce 'Theotokos,' so that, a mixture having taken place and the natures not being divided, none of the lowly things may be ascribed to the humanity, and they may then have room to attack the Godhead, as though everything said were said of one." Since this is what was said, the anathema we composed was most useful, for it does not permit the one Lord Jesus Christ to be divided into two persons and hypostases. [Notes: "Aim, as" [?]; "of the things said"; "most usefully"; [?]; "about".]

And that they agree with our very words is surely clear from what they have written and resolved to hold. It runs thus: "Now, one must not apply the expressions by dividing the union, that is, the one Son, into two persons, or hypostases, or two sons; for the supreme union is indivisible and inseparable, and the one Son is one in every respect, in principle, manner and concept. But while the supreme union is safeguarded, and the one Son, Christ and Lord is confessed, what is said must be understood of one and the same Son. Yet it is fitting that what is said be applied to the one Son according to the power of the united natures." So then, if the union to the utmost degree is preserved, what entry for division, or even the notion of it, could still creep in? And how can the one who dares to divide not stray from the straight road and wholly depart from the doctrines of true religion? What, then, does the anathema say? If anyone divides the expressions in this way, attaching some to a man thought of separately apart from the Word from God, and others, as befitting God, to the Word from God alone, let him be anathema. If, then, those who separate and distinguish them, assigning some to a man individually and separately and others to God the Word individually and separately, are not dividing the one Christ and speaking of two sons, let these lovers of accusation be angry with us. But if to think this way is cutting and division, on what ground have they resolved to censure our words, when they themselves, as they say, confess that Emmanuel is undivided and one by supreme union? Now, that each expression must be understood with discernment, even if it happens to be spoken by him himself, I would commend myself, as I think would everyone accustomed to right thinking; for some are befitting God, while others are better suited to the economy in the flesh. But since he is one and the same, God and man together, for that very reason he quite rightly speaks sometimes as God and sometimes as man. Yet we insist that both kinds are the expressions of the one Jesus Christ, neither stripping the temple born of the all-holy Virgin of the Godhead, nor regarding the Word from God the Father as fleshless after the ineffable union. I am amazed that, though they are extremely meddlesome and, as they think, subtly scrutinize my letters, they deliberately pass over everything in them that is useful and necessary to prove the correctness and precision of the doctrines, but pounce eagerly on anything that has, in their opinion, even a faint ground for suspicion, so as to use it to make false accusations against us. I will recall my own words. For I wrote thus in the letter to Nestorius: "The expressions of our Saviour in the Gospels we neither [divide] between two persons [Notes: "Son" [?]; "to understand"; "as anyone"; "not separating"; "not two"; "of the sayings".]

…into two hypostases, nor do we divide him into two persons. The one and only Christ is not twofold, even if he is conceived of as brought together out of two different realities into an indivisible unity. In the same way, a human being is conceived of as made of soul and body, yet is not twofold but one out of both. Thinking rightly, we will hold that both the human sayings and the divine ones were spoken by one and the same. When he speaks of himself in a way that befits God, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father,” and “I and the Father are one,” we understand his divine and ineffable nature. In that nature, because his substance is the same as the Father's, he is the image and exact imprint of his own Father and the radiance of his glory. But when he does not scorn the measure of humanity and says to the Jews, “But now you are seeking to kill me, a man who has told you the truth,” we still recognize him, even from the measures of his humanity, as God the Word, equal to and like the Father. If we must believe that he who is God by nature became flesh, that is, a man, with the flesh given life by a rational soul, what reason could anyone have to be ashamed of his sayings when they are spoken in a way that befits a man? If he refused words that befit a man, who forced him to become a man like us? And if he lowered himself for our sake into a voluntary self-emptying, why would he refuse the words that befit that self-emptying? All the sayings in the Gospels must therefore be attributed to one person, to the one incarnate hypostasis of the Word. For according to the Scriptures there is one Lord Jesus Christ. From what has already been written, then, no one will catch us ignorant of the economy, or of which saying befits each nature. Rather, we will not allow the unspiritual, who do not have the Spirit, to think or speak of two sons by dividing the hypostases from one another after the inseparable union. Now they have taken a small part of our letter and placed it at the beginning of their own treatise. They threaten to refute us in due course, claiming that we have sinned gravely against the Word from God the Father by most foolishly attributing to his nature the growth and progress that belong to the flesh. Come, then, let us say what is fitting in reply to this as well, and set out the whole passage of the letter. They fear the truth, and they carry their hearers along with them, so they quoted only the part that seemed most useful to them for making their slanders against us, and for making those slanders look reasonable. The passage runs as follows: “Even if you hear that Jesus advanced in stature and wisdom and grace, do not think that the Word of God became wise by making progress; [Variant readings: “twofold, but rather one”; “Christ”; “and as”; “undivided”; “fearing”; [?] “yes”; “to approve”, “reasonably”.]

remember instead that the divine Paul wrote: ‘Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.’ Do not foolishly dare to say either that we attach the advance in stature, wisdom and grace to the man. That, I think, is nothing other than dividing the one Christ into two. As I said just now, he is the Son before the ages, yet he is said to have been designated Son of God in the last times of the age, because in the economy he made the birth of his own flesh his own. In the same way he is the Wisdom of the one who begot him, yet he is said to advance in wisdom. As God he is entirely perfect, but because of the supreme union he fittingly takes the properties of humanity to himself.” Why, then, when God says, “Judge a righteous judgment,” do they misrepresent the truth? We do not teach that the hypostases are divided after the union, and we do not say that the nature of the Godhead needed growth and progress. Rather, we say that by an appropriation that belongs to the economy he made the properties of the flesh his own, since he became flesh, according to the Scriptures. The choir of the holy Fathers agrees with this faith and teaching, and I will try to show it. For full assurance I will set out part of a sermon once given by Atticus of blessed memory. It runs as follows. Atticus, bishop of Constantinople: “Today Christ the Master accepted the birth that comes from his love for humankind, for he already possessed the birth that belongs to his divine dignity.” Then he adds: “The Word who loves humankind is emptied, though by nature he cannot be emptied. ‘For he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.’ The fleshless one takes flesh for your sake. ‘For the Word became flesh.’ He who cannot be touched, because his nature is bodiless, is handled. He who has no beginning comes under a bodily beginning. The perfect one grows. The unchangeable one advances. The rich one is found in an inn. He who covers heaven with clouds is wrapped in swaddling cloths. The king is laid in a manger.” Dividing the hypostases after the union is not blameless. It belongs rather to those who overturn the holy mystery of the incarnation. We will see this just as clearly by reading the passages set out here from Julius and Felix, who in their day presided over the Church of the Romans. Julius, bishop of Rome: “For the completion of the faith we proclaim also that the Son of God was made flesh from the Virgin Mary and dwelt among human beings. He did not merely work in a man, as in the case of the prophets and apostles. He is perfect God in the flesh and perfect man in the Spirit. There are not two sons, one a genuine Son who assumed a man, and the other a mortal man assumed by God. There is one Only-begotten in heaven, who is also the Only-begotten God on earth.”

“Concerning the incarnation of the Word and the faith: we believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin Mary. Being perfect God, he became at the same time perfect man, made flesh from…

ANATHEMA 7. If anyone says that Jesus, as a man, was empowered by God the Word, and that the glory of the Only-begotten was attached to him as to someone existing besides him, let him be anathema. Objection of the Easterners. No one would [?] confess that our Lord Jesus Christ was empowered by the Spirit simply as a man, or as a prophet, or as an apostle.
