Nor do we erase or deny the divine sayings, or ignorantly and blasphemously anathematize them, since they were spoken and recorded because of the nature of the visible flesh. Nor will we say that he was empowered simply as a man, or as a righteous man, a prophet or an apostle. He did not say, “Thus says the Lord.” He spoke as the Son giving the law: “But I say…

Defense of Cyril. Here too our defense proceeds along the same lines as before. Our Lord Jesus Christ is acknowledged to be one. We believe that the same one is the eternal Word from God the Father, existing before the ages, and that in the last times of the age he became a man from a woman, born in the flesh in a marvelous way. Being one Son, God and Lord, he worked the divine signs through a strength beyond human power. In this way he made it certain that, even though he became flesh, he is still true God and the power of the Father. For he did not cease to be what he was when he became [Variant readings: “again we shall erase”; [?] “him”; “then the”; “then”.]

man. So he performed the wonders: at one moment rebuking demons and crushing Satan, at another giving light to the blind and raising the dead, or calming the raging sea with a single word. He was not causing some man, a separate Christ existing apart, to be glorified, as would happen with one of the holy prophets or apostles. He was gaining the glory for himself, so that all would believe that he is God by nature, even though he became man. It was therefore utterly outrageous to put up with Nestorius when he said: “The operations of the Trinity are common and are distinguished only by the hypostases. So the glory of the Only-begotten is attached sometimes to the Father, sometimes to the Spirit, and sometimes to the power of Christ.” Let those who want to find fault, then, do one of two things. They can show us another Christ, existing and conceived of separately and on his own, to whom the only-begotten Word of God attached his own power, as though this Son were someone other than himself. Or, if he is not one and then another, but one and the same, only-begotten from the Father and man from a woman according to the flesh, how could it have been right to choose silence? Was it not right instead to raise the power of the truth once again against his babblings, which disfigure the beauty of the doctrines of true religion? The Son was God and is God. But once he entered the measure of humanity, he did not treat the economy as something to be discarded. He willingly endured everything for our sake because of the self-emptying. For this reason, although he is life by nature, he is said to be given life by the Father, and although he is the Lord of glory, he is said to receive glory. So the Hebrew of Hebrews, a true scholar of the law, of the tribe of Benjamin, said: “Paul, an apostle, not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead” and gave him glory. He is said to receive glory from the Father, because the matter comes down to the measure of humanity. Yet he knows that, in so far as he is God and is conceived of as God, he has what is above creation. He says: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father. No one knows who the Son is except the Father, and no one knows who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.” But one of the more studious might say: “If all things were handed over to you by the Father, as to someone who needed glory and had to receive power over all things as a gift because of your humanity, how can you say that human minds cannot attain the knowledge of you, just as they cannot attain the knowledge of the Father?” “Yes,” he says, “but the knowledge of me is not confined to what is seen. I am God in flesh and blood. I am known through the flesh. But in the nature and glory of the Godhead I am equal in measure to [Variant readings: “raising”; “or of apostles”; “the Son individually; or if”.]

God the Father, and I go beyond all mind and reason.” So, to keep to the sense of the passage before us, we do not do away with the apostolic sayings. God forbid! Nor do we oppose the principles of the incarnation by thinking or saying anything improper. We follow the sacred Scriptures everywhere and grant that the sayings of those who spoke for God must prevail. We stand against only those who distort the right doctrines of the Church. No one would doubt that the Father is said to have raised our Lord Jesus Christ from the dead, since the act obviously concerned his flesh. Yet he himself, being the life and the life-giving, active power of the Father, gave life to his own temple. “Destroy this temple,” he says, “and in three days I will raise it up.” So it was…

…We do not speak of being “worshiped together” and “glorified together” as though there were two persons, or hypostases, or sons, with worship offered to the flesh in one way and to God the Word in another. Rather, we offer one worship, and everything else, as to one Son, and we speak of his being “worshiped together” just as he himself says in his first book: “Although as the Word he always sits with his own Father, and exists by nature from him and in him, he again heard the Father say to him, now with the flesh: ‘Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.’ In the same way we say that he is worshiped both by us and by the holy angels.” Our reply is that he has very cleverly condemned those who wish to worship the one and same Son together with the flesh. He writes as though “together with” (syn) were something different from “with” (meta), the word he himself used, as mentioned above, when he said that the Son must be worshiped with the flesh, while forbidding the flesh to be worshiped together with the Godhead. Defense of Cyril. The divine Paul makes us most prudent when he says: “Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith.” For the human mind, out of self-love, [Variant readings: “destroy the temple” [?]; “kindles” or “sends up”; “saying”; “most prudently”.]

sometimes strays from the straight road and moves away from the doctrines of the truth, yet it always somehow hesitates and fears to recognize how discordant its own ideas are. It will correct itself quite easily, however, by studying the labors of the holy Fathers, who are renowned among all for the orthodoxy and precision of their doctrines. Then it will test its own faith skillfully, for all who are sound of mind aim to follow the teachings of the Fathers. They filled their own minds with the apostolic and evangelical tradition, and they set out the teaching about the faith rightly and blamelessly from the sacred Scriptures. So they were lights in the world, holding fast the word of life, as it is written. Our father and bishop Athanasius, of eternal memory, writes about Christ, the Savior of us all, in his work on the incarnation: “We confess that he is the Son of God and God according to the Spirit, and son of man according to the flesh. The one Son is not two natures, one to be worshiped and one not to be worshiped. He is one nature of God the Word, made flesh, worshiped together with his flesh in one act of worship. Nor are there two sons, one the true Son of God, who is worshiped, and the other the man from Mary, who is not worshiped and became a son of God by grace, as human beings do.” And again, after other things: “He who was born of the Virgin Mary is Son of God by nature and true God, not by grace and participation. He is man only in respect of the flesh that came from Mary, but in respect of the Spirit he himself is Son of God and God.” And again: “If anyone teaches something different from this, from the divine Scriptures, and says that the Son of God is one person and the one from Mary another, made a son by grace as we are, so that there are two sons, one Son of God by nature, from God, and the other the man from Mary, a son by grace; or if anyone says that the flesh of our Lord came from above and not from the Virgin Mary; or that the Godhead was changed into flesh, or mixed, or altered; or that the Godhead of the Lord could suffer; or that the flesh of our Lord, as the flesh of a man, is not to be worshiped, rather than worshiped as the flesh of the Lord and God: such a person the holy and catholic Church anathematizes, obeying the divine Apostle, who says, ‘If anyone preaches to you a gospel other than the one you received, let him be anathema.’” This is what that man believed and wrote for us. Yet Nestorius, who has chosen to make war on the glory of Christ and has let his unbridled tongue loose against him, says somewhere: “We confess the God in the man. We revere the man who, through the divine conjunction, is worshiped together with God the Word.” Does he not plainly call Christ a God-bearing man, and say that a man simply came into conjunction [Variant readings: “perhaps, the teaching about the faith”; “of celebrated memory”; “having written”; “it”.]

with God, perhaps in the sense of the saying spoken by Paul: “Whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit with him”? Yet it is surely true that the same one is God and man at once. He is not some man conceived of on his own, as an individual, who has only a relational conjunction with God. After the ineffable union, if anyone calls Emmanuel, who became man and was made flesh, God, we should understand the Word of God. And if anyone calls him man, we know that he is also, together with this, the Word of the Father. It is one thing, then, to say that the Word from God the Father is one Son together with the flesh united to him. It is quite another to say that God is in a man, as he was in the prophets, or indeed in us through the Holy Spirit. I think one could say, without danger and without reproach, that the incarnate Word of God, being one Son, is to be worshiped not apart from his own flesh but rather with it. In the same way, a human soul is honored together with its own body, and what is made of both is signified by a single name, as one living being. Suppose, then, that in your eagerness to speak about Christ, the Savior of us all, you divide [?] the one into two and declare that there is a man, conceived of individually and on his own. Suppose you then dare to say that this man must be worshiped together with Christ, the Son from God by nature, and called God together with him, as though Christ existed alongside him as someone else. Who could bear that? Who could pass over in silence such blatant idle talk against him? He ought rather to have said: “We revere the Word of God who became man, who is called God and worshiped [?] in his humanity, because he is God by nature and has appeared from God the Father.” “Yes,” say our opponents, “but you too will be caught out, since you wrote in a letter that the Son sat with the Father with his own flesh. How then can you criticize someone who says that the man must be worshiped together with God the Word and called God together with him? To say ‘together with’ and to say ‘with’ is the same thing.” Let us show, then, that they do not understand the force of these words and do not look into the nature of things. Take the case of one person and nature, that is, one hypostasis. When the discussion examines the parts that make it up, the parts of which it is naturally composed, and adds “together with” or “with,” it preserves the meaning that the thing is one by composition, and it will not separate it into two divided beings. But when “together with” or “with” is said of hypostases already divided into two, each of which must be conceived of separately and individually, then we say that the words indicate two, or even more, and not one by composition. For example, suppose we said that a person's soul is honored together with its own body, if there should be [?] [Variant readings: [?]; “in silence”; “I revere”; “as somewhere”.]

from him an honor paid to the one human being, who is made of both. Or suppose someone says that the soul is one living being together with its own body. He will certainly not divide the one into two human beings. Rather, he shows that he understands the parts of which a human being is made, that is, of which it is naturally composed. But when I say, “Peter and John are together called men,” or “John went up to the temple with Peter,” the words “together with” and “with” no longer indicate one. Peter is not compounded with John, and the two together do not make up a single human being. Why, then, do they play the sophist against the truth and ignorantly divide the one Christ into two? Do they think that by saying that the Son sits with the Father with his own body, we have allowed two sons to be conceived? Then let them examine whether, in speaking of one Son, we say that he is honored with one sharing of the throne, rather than two, as though one sharing were assigned to the body on its own and another to the Word on its own. They could not show this. How could they, or [?]? We firmly affirm that the Son, who is one Son together with his own flesh, the same one being God and man at once, is honored with one sharing of the Father's throne. But to say that a man is worshiped together with God and called God together with him is surely to confess two who are worshiped, or who are called God together with each other. Such a statement is extremely simple-minded and entirely foreign to thoughts that aim at correctness and truth. The anathema was therefore made against those who completely divide Emmanuel into a man on his own and God the Word on his own. For the teaching of those who spoke for God, and the genuine knowledge of the sacred Scriptures, proclaimed him to us as one.

ANATHEMA 9. If anyone says that the one Lord Jesus Christ was glorified by the Spirit, as though he used through him a power foreign to himself, and received from him the ability to act against unclean spirits and to perform divine signs among human beings, and does not say instead that the Spirit through whom he worked the divine signs is his own, let him be anathema. Objection of the Easterners. It is good, once again, to bring into the open what he said long ago, and to remind him of himself, since perhaps he has forgotten. He declared not only that the Lord performed the signs in the Spirit, but also that after he died he was made alive by the Spirit. He says in his first book: “If, then, he did not undergo death in the flesh according to the Scriptures, neither was he made alive by the Spirit.” We must notice how he contradicts himself. In his anathemas he forbade anyone to say that the Lord cast out demons and performed the other signs by the Spirit of God, and the Lord's written saying recorded in the Gospels [Variant readings: “by him”; “you play the sophist”; “worship. and”.]

[?] rejecting [?]. When he said, "But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God." We, however, confess that our Lord Jesus Christ performed the signs both by his own power and by the working of the Spirit. For to say that he used the power of the Holy Spirit as one who had no power of his own, and that the Holy Spirit is not one with him, is, I think, the mark of those who deny the divine Scriptures. For even if the divine Scripture somewhere says that the Father performs the works of the miracles, as where it says, "The Father who abides in me, he does the works that I do," it is the Son who does all the works of the Father. And even if it says that the Spirit does the works of the Son, as where it says, "But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God," it is the Lord who does them in the Spirit. For the Son is not estranged from the Father or from the Spirit, nor are the workings of the Trinity ever separated and peculiar to one person. Rather, the working that Scripture ascribes to each hypostasis belongs to the Trinity. In the same way Scripture sometimes calls the whole creation the work of the Son, saying, "By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made firm," and sometimes the work of the Spirit, where it adds, "and all their host by the Spirit of his mouth." Yet the Son does not also create because the Father is unable to make all things, nor again is the Spirit brought in to help because the Son is too weak for the work of creation (for it is true that "All things came into being through him"). Rather, to show us that the Trinity is of one essence, equal in honour and equal in power, Scripture says that the same things came into being sometimes by the Father, sometimes by the Son, and sometimes by the Holy Spirit. In this way we understand that all things depend on one divine essence. For just as the Only-begotten, possessing the essence and subsisting as a hypostasis, was begotten of him without passion, so the Spirit too, proceeding from him, exists in its own hypostasis. Thus one essence is marked out in three hypostases, and none of them is seen as estranged from the others in the definition of the essence; they are distinguished from one another only by their characteristic, or rather distinguishing, properties. How then can there be a separate working in those whose essence, power and will are one? For where these things are shared, there is wholly one

Cyril's Defence. Shall I need the testimony of witnesses to show that our opponents like to talk idly and thoughtlessly heap slanders on us? I think their own statement alone will prove it. In the anathema before us we stated plainly that the Holy Spirit is the Son's own, and indeed that he performed the divine signs through him. But they, though they keep insisting that I have forgotten my own words, [Notes: Matt. 12:28. John 14:10. Matt. [?]. Variant: "for as the word".]

have themselves sunk to such dullness and stupidity that they think I say Jesus did not cast out demons through the Spirit. Is this not plain slander? If they do not think casting out demons counts as a divine sign, they may say what they like: let them bring a charge against me on that score and accuse me of not having said this clearly and of passing over the divine signs in silence. But if casting out demons, along with the rest, is a kind of divine sign, and no unremarkable one, why have they thrown away the choice of speaking well as worthless, and set aside the duty of speaking the truth as stale? Why have they valued unbridled abuse of us so highly, and thought it no small matter, though it is so condemned both by God [?] and by men? They seem to me to have forgotten Christ's words: "How can you say to your brother, 'Brother, let me take the speck out of your eye,' when there is a log in your own eye? Hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye." That the Holy Trinity is of one essence, equal in strength and equal in working, we did not learn from what you say; we were fully assured of it rather from the divinely inspired Scripture. And it is easy to see that the anathema before us in no way harms the teachings of the right faith but rather serves them. As we have already said many times, there are those who divide the one Lord Jesus Christ and split him into a man on his own and God the Word on his own, so that two persons and two hypostases are understood, standing apart from one another. The anathema does not allow them to do this. Nor does it permit them to say that Jesus, as an ordinary man, was empowered by the Spirit so that he could perform the divine signs. For then he would differ in no way from the holy apostles, or indeed from the prophets, who, filled from above with the kindness of the divine gifts, might rightly say, "By the grace of God we are what we are." Such words would rightly suit the holy men to whom gifts from God are distributed, but not Christ. For the Holy Spirit is his own, just as he is also the Spirit of God the Father; and as the Father works through the Spirit, so does he. And indeed, though he said to the Jews, "I have shown you many good works from my Father," and, "I do not speak on my own; the Father who abides in me does the works himself," he also said elsewhere, "But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God," ascribing the working through the Spirit both to himself and to the Father because they are identical in essence. The discussion of these matters could become extensive and long;

but those who wish to expand on it need, I think, the proper occasion. So we do not say that Emmanuel was empowered by the power that comes through the Spirit as though it were a power alien to him. We say rather that he used it as God, and that the power of the Spirit, who is of one essence with him, is his own. When the blessed disciples performed signs, they said, "Men, why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we had made the lame man who sat at the Beautiful Gate walk?" But the Spirit of Christ is his own. To those who wish to scrutinize what we say, we say this: if they see nothing wrong in dividing the indivisible and saying that Jesus was empowered through the Spirit as an ordinary man, the argument with people of that mind will be a long one. But if they confess that Christ is one, both Son and Lord, the same being God and man together, let them believe with us that he was not empowered through the Spirit by a power greater than himself and alien to him. Let them believe rather that he himself performed the divine sign, as through his own Spirit, in whom lies all the power of created things. Then they will stop their pointless abuse and stop sinking the teeth of envy into us.

ANATHEMA 10. The divine Scripture says that Christ became the High Priest and Apostle of our confession, and that he offered himself for us to God the Father as a fragrant aroma. If anyone, then, says that our High Priest and Apostle was not the very Word from God the Father, when he became flesh and a man like us, but as it were someone other than him, a man on his own, born of a woman; or if anyone says that he offered the sacrifice for himself as well, and not rather for us alone (for he who knew no sin would have had no need of a sacrifice), let him be anathema. Refutation by the Easterners. If God the Word is high priest, to which God of his, or to what kind of God, does he offer worship? He has forgotten the blessed Paul, who said, "For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who has been tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin." Who then is the one who was tempted? God the Word, or the human nature, the seed of David? And again: "No one takes this honour for himself, but he is called by God, just as Aaron was. So also Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest." Who then is compared with Aaron in the dignity of the priesthood, and with one who does not take the honour for himself, but is called by God and rises to the dignity of the priesthood?
[Variant readings:] a "but there is need, I think"; b "to direct"; "they confess"; "is empowered"; "but he works"; "that"; "and for"; "he took hold of"; "but the one"; "and Aaron".

Is it the divine nature, which is coeternal with the Father and has all that belongs to the Father? To what dignity greater than itself did it rise? Am I to say that the priesthood is worthier than the divine nature, so that he rose to it not of himself but called by God, and was glorified by it? Or is it the nature that came from the seed of David and was appointed, to which God swore, according to the Psalmist, to give the priesthood forever? "For the Lord has sworn," it says, "and will not change his mind: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek." Did the divinity of the Only-begotten receive sworn promises from God that it would receive the priesthood forever and be glorified by it? Who would put up with us if we said or thought such things? Who would not despise us for presenting God as ordained high priest, receiving sworn promises, called to the dignity of the priesthood, not taking the honour for himself but called to it, and compared with the first man to receive the priesthood? And again it says, as it also says in another place, "You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek." And again, who is likened to Melchizedek in priesthood? Is it reverent to suppose it is God, or rather the flesh taken from us, which was united inseparably and joined without confusion? And again it says: "In the days of his flesh he offered up prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears to the one who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence." Did God the Word offer prayers and supplications with loud cries to someone able to save him, and was he heard because of his reverence, and did he learn obedience from what he suffered? If God the Word is high priest, then he himself also learned from what he suffered and was made perfect. But do not let your minds be troubled when you hear it said of the one who suffered, "although he was a Son." For we do not speak of two sons, one who suffered and one who remained beyond suffering. The Son from the seed of David is not so named separately and apart from the divinity, just as the divinity after the union is not called Son without the visible flesh. For after the union the sonship is one for both natures, which are not separated from one another. For no separation [?] came about after the union, since the union remains forever. Even in the sufferings of the flesh the divinity was inseparable, while remaining impassible, and what befits God was accomplished through the flesh. Hence we confess one and the same Son, the natures remaining unconfused, not saying one and another, God forbid, but one and the same. That our Lord Jesus Christ, then, became our High Priest and Apostle

according to the divine Scriptures, no one would refuse to confess. It is not, however, a man born of a woman, separated on his own from the Word of God the Father. Rather, the one from the seed of David, united without confusion, ineffably and inseparably with the Word from the Father, is the High Priest who was tempted in all things without sin, who learned obedience from what he suffered, and who offered his own flesh to God the Father, not for himself but for us alone. For we will not ignorantly say that God the Word is high priest and that he offered himself to God the Father; for the Father is not the God of the divinity of the Only-begotten, but its Father. Cyril's Defence. Once again it will be fitting for us to say to our opponents, "How long will you go limping on both legs?" For you ought to keep your minds sound and whole for an exact knowledge of the straight path of doctrine, not limping with double-mindedness, nor sick with great weakness and unable to walk upright. "For the double-minded man is unstable in all his ways, and he will receive nothing from the Lord." I say this because I am greatly amazed at our opponents, who so shamelessly and rashly want to attack the present anathema too. Yet it is no wonder if they do not want us to call the Word from God the Father the Apostle and High Priest of our confession, when he became man. For those who try to slander his birth according to the flesh altogether, who have dared to reject it as untrue, and who will not tolerate calling the holy Virgin Theotokos, how will they not reject the ways of the dispensation? Let them hear, then, what was said through the voice of Isaiah: "If you do not believe, you will not understand." The inspired evangelist John thundered out something great and extraordinary to all under heaven when he said that the Word became flesh. But they, stealthily robbing the truth of its force, say he became flesh in the sense in which he might be understood to have become a curse and sin. We have already spoken about this earlier, in terms that could fairly show their argument on these points to be stale. But to these fault-finders we now say this: Learn to listen, you who are narrow of heart. Accept the foundation of the mystery of Christ, the first principles of the dispensation and, so to speak, its very entrance. Believe with us, or rather with the holy Scriptures. Cast your vote for the truth, confessing that the only-begotten Word of God himself, who is in the bosom of the Father, through whom are all things and in whom are all things, became [Variant readings: "own"; "sound"; "for I am greatly amazed at the".]

flesh. He did not undergo change or mixture, but always remained by nature what he was, and is, and will be. He became flesh by undergoing birth from the holy Virgin, birth according to the flesh, I mean; he was called Son of Man, and he shared in blood and flesh just as we do. To those of this mind, who have received this most venerable and true faith, all that follows will seem easy going, a road fit for riding, with nothing steep or rough. For it is written that all things are plain to those who understand, and right to those who find knowledge. Now I think we must also state the reason the anathema was written. Nestorius, who stirred everything up and turned everything upside down, said something like this about Christ, the Saviour of us all: (He was sent to proclaim release to the captives, this one who was made a faithful high priest to God. For he became this; he was not this eternally. This is the one, O heretic, who advanced little by little to the dignity of high priest.) He adds many other things that give birth to an impiety akin to this. Who, hearing such shameful words, would not choose to suffer anything rather than cherish the silence that God abhors? Christ died for us; despising the shame, he endured the cross and death according to the flesh. Shall we then not repay our benefactor even with goodwill in words, but sit quietly listening to such outrageous blasphemies, or perhaps even share in the guilt of the tongue that rails against him? What are you saying, sir? He advanced little by little to become high priest? And yet the Word, being God, emptied himself; he who is free by nature took the form of a slave; he who is beyond every created thing and glories in the heights of divinity humbled himself. If he advanced, in what way was he emptied? Or how did he lower himself to humility? Would anyone say that the emptying won him honour and glory, as a matchmaker wins a bride? Then how is emptying still an advancement [?]? "Yes," he says, "but if the very Word from God the Father became high priest, who then is greater than he, and receives the worship of his priestly service?" I will say something again, then: Believe that although the Son was God by nature and in the form of the Father, he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave. If he became man and took the form of a slave, how could he think it beneath him, or out of keeping with the purposes of the dispensation, to be called both apostle and high priest? And how could he who did not disdain the measure of our humanity reject what is human? It would perhaps be no hard task to go through still more arguments and draw out the account at greater length. But I will leave this for now and set out the words they themselves have written. They wrote as follows:

"But do not let your minds be troubled when you hear it said of the one who suffered, 'although he was a Son.' For we do not speak of two sons, one who suffered and one who remained beyond suffering. The Son from the seed of David is not so named separately and apart from the divinity, just as the divinity after the union is not called Son without the visible flesh." And again: "Hence we confess one and the same Son, the natures remaining unconfused, not saying one and another, God forbid, but one and the same. That our Lord Jesus Christ, then, became our High Priest and Apostle according to the divine Scriptures, no one would refuse to confess; not, however, a man born of a woman separated on his own from the Word from God the Father." If, then, they say there is one Son, and in no way divide him into two, the one from the seed of David and the Word from God the Father, how are they not wronging the mystery by dividing the dispensation between God and a man? Why do they not rather say that one and the same is both God and man, so that everything is his, both what befits God and what is human? Whenever something supremely befitting God is said of him, we say it is wholly true, for we know him to be God. And if something human is said, we will agree to that as well, for we confess that he is God in flesh and blood, and we recognize the measure of his humanity through what is human. Thousands upon thousands of holy angels minister to him, and the Seraphim stand around his divine throne. But since he became man, he was also called high priest. He does not offer the sacred service to a greater God, but carries out the confession of our faith to himself and to the Father. Do you blush to hear that he was called priest because of his humanity? Then why are you not amazed that he does not, as priests usually do, perform the sacred service to another, but rather, as I said, to himself and to the Father? When you say it is unworthy of God to perform sacred service, I agree. If the Word were alone and without flesh, you would be right. But since he became man, see him performing sacred service because of his humanity, and yet, as God, holding dignities above all creation; for he shares the throne of God the Father. See him, then, acting as priest according to his humanity, but sharing the throne as God. For what does the blessed Paul say? "We have such a high priest, one who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty on high." Knowing, then, that being God he became man, and that he is one and the same Son, we will ascribe everything to him as to one. And we will not be ignorant of the ways of the dispensation, but will always skilfully and wisely turn the force of our thoughts round to obedience to him.

ANATHEMA 11. If anyone does not confess that the flesh of the Lord is life-giving and the very own flesh of the Word from God the Father, [Variant readings: "hearing"; "performs"; "we will be ignorant of"; "looking around", or "tending".]

…but as of someone other than him, joined to him by dignity, or as having only a divine indwelling, and not rather life-giving, as we said, because it became the very own flesh of the Word who has power to give life to all things: let him be anathema.

Objection of the Orientals. It is right to confess that the Lord's flesh became the Word's own through the union, provided we understand that it was taken from us. But it is superfluous to add "and not of someone other than him," unless he is in fact excluding it from having been taken from us. For to keep calling it "his own" is the mark of one who excludes the Lord's flesh from belonging to our nature. And where is our boast? Through whom, says Paul, did he raise us up with him and seat us with him? And whose flesh, among other human beings, is each person's flesh? Does not each of us have flesh that is common to every other, by reason of our sharing one substance, and also his own, in that each person's flesh belongs to no one else but only to him whose flesh it is? What then does he mean by "his own," as though he were saying something different? For if he understands that the Lord's flesh was taken from ours, and understands that each person's flesh is the own flesh of the one whose flesh it is and of no one else, why does he call it "his own" as though it were not foreign [?]? Or is it clear that, under a veil, he is saying that it was not taken from our nature? He says this more plainly in his first tome: "And the infant," he says, "was [not?] like us [?]; that is, not in bare and mere likeness to us, but in humanity, because of the flesh, yet divine, as being above us and from heaven." And again in the second tome, where he says: "For the body born of her was not that of someone other, one of those like us, but rather the own body of the Word himself, who is from [the Father?] [?]." Who ever said that the Lord's flesh belonged to some other of the human beings who have lived from the beginning of time, say Abel, or Noah, or Elijah, or any other of the human beings from the beginning of time? We declare not only of the Lord's flesh that it did not belong to some other of the human beings from the beginning of time, but was the Lord's own and his alone, united without confusion and without separation to God the Word; but also that the flesh of each one of us has never belonged, as we said, to anyone other than him whose flesh it is. Since, then, this is confessed by all members of the Church, what does he mean by constantly calling it "his own," unless he is excluding it from belonging to our nature? And how does he forbid saying that it was joined to him by dignity and authority, when he himself says in the first tome: "For thus we too have been made rich by his poverty, human nature having been raised up in him to a dignity befitting God"? But let us say to him, since he contradicts even himself: If, then, the natures remain unconfused, and the union remains common [?]… [Variant readings (?): "the union; and we say the… own"; "seated with, and".]

…in worship, power, dignity, and authority, such as is fitting to be offered to one Son, while the natures remain unconfused in the union: what else is left that characterizes the union more precisely? We will grant it and agree to it, short of confusing the natures. But it is evident that, unless he confuses the natures, nothing satisfies him as the height of union. We, however, will keep the natures unconfused, and we confess the union to be the highest, divine, and incomprehensible to us, offering everything in glorification as to God and one Son, and saying to him the words of blessed Peter: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God."

Defense of Cyril. Once the crowds of the Jews were whetted to unholy fury, their minds shot through with the arrows of envy. And since, besides this, they were also laying their profane hands on Christ, the Savior of us all, he bade them state the reasons for such outrages, saying: "I have shown you many good works from my Father; for which of these works are you stoning me?" But they came to such a pitch of perverse counsel and unholy thinking that they even tried to entangle him in charges of blasphemy. For they said: "We are not stoning you for a good work, but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God." And the Savior said to them: "Is it not written in your law, I said, You are gods? If he called them gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken—do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, You are blaspheming, because I said, I am the Son of God?" Now as we inquire into the manner of the sending spoken of here, we gather our knowledge on this point from the holy Scriptures. He himself said, then, through the voice of Isaiah: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the poor, to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind." We say that the Son was sent by the Father when he became man; for both the name and the fact of being sent would quite rightly suit the measures of the self-emptying. And the Word from God the Father was sent, as I said, not naked and fleshless; rather, he underwent birth according to the flesh, that is, he took a body from the holy Virgin and united it to himself ineffably and without confusion, as we have said very many times, and so "God the Lord appeared to us," according to the Scriptures. We say, therefore, that the body became the Word's own, and not the body of some man individually and separately conceived as another Christ and Son besides him. And just as the body that belongs particularly to each of us is called his own, so also… [Variant readings (?): "perhaps 'or'"; "which… a more precise… the"; "let us keep".]

…must it be understood in the case of the one Christ. For even though it is of the same kind as our bodies, that is, of the same substance (for he was born of a woman), it is understood and called his own, as I said. And since the Word from God the Father is life by nature, he made his own flesh life-giving; for this reason it has become for us a life-giving blessing. And indeed Christ said: "Truly, truly, I say to you, I am the living bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world"; and again: "And the bread that I will give is my flesh, for the life of the world." And again: "He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him." Observe, then, how everywhere he calls the body born of a woman his own, because of the highest union. Although this is the meaning of the mystery, Nestorius again says in a commentary of his own: "Listen, then, paying attention to the words: 'He who eats my flesh,' he says. Remember that what is said concerns the flesh, and that the word 'flesh' was not added by me, so that I may not seem to them to be misinterpreting. 'He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood.' Did he say, 'He who eats my divinity and drinks my divinity'? 'He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.' Remember that what is said concerns the flesh. But perhaps I am misinterpreting. Let us listen to what follows: 'As the living Father sent me.' He says it means the divinity; I say the humanity. Let us see who is the misinterpreter. 'As the living Father sent me.' Here the heretic says it means the divinity. Does he say, 'The living Father sent me, God the Word'? According to them, then, 'And I, God the Word, live because of the Father'? Then after this, again: 'He who eats me, he too will live.' Whom do we eat? The divinity, or the flesh?" Now about these outlandish things, so carelessly babbled by him, we have already spoken at length. But what he could mean, when he says that it was not God the Word, incarnate and made man, who was sent, but again posits separately and apart, as he himself puts it, the one who appeared, I cannot say. Or rather, the sophistry is already plain. For he dissolves the manner of the union so that the body of Christ may turn out to be common, and no longer truly the own body of him who has power to give life to all things. Admittedly, all human things are small for God the Word; but since for our sake he deigned to undergo the self-emptying that saved the world, even if he is said to have been sent to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, he is all the more glorified for having taken upon himself the lowliness of the economy in the flesh. And no one of sound mind, I think, would find fault with him for having lowered himself into our condition for our sake. Is it not, then, by affirming that the one who appeared is some other Son and Christ besides the Word from God… [Variant reading: "would find fault".]

…—the one to whom alone he has assigned the business of being sent—that he makes our mystery out to be cannibalism, unholily leading the minds of believers into debased notions, and trying to subject to human reasonings what is received only by a [?] and unquestioning faith? For no one could say that, because the nature of the divinity is not eaten, the holy body of Christ is therefore common. Rather, one must know that, as we said before, it is the own body of the Word who gives life to all things; and since it is the body of life, it is life-giving. For through it he instills life into our mortal bodies, so that he also abolishes the power of death. And in the same way the Holy Spirit of Christ also gives us life; for it is the Spirit who gives life, according to the very words of the Savior. And so that I may not seem to be the only one who calls the body the Word's own, nothing prevents me from also setting out the testimonies of the holy Fathers, so that our opponents may see that they have railed against us in vain, since we follow their words in everything. Our all-praised father and bishop Athanasius, then, said in his discourse on the Trinity: "And it was shown that he had a body not in appearance but truly. For it was fitting that the Lord, in putting on human flesh, should put it on whole, with its own passions, so that, just as we say that the body is his own, so also the passions of the body may be said to be his alone, even though they did not touch him in his divinity." And again: "We have necessarily examined these things beforehand, so that if we see him acting or speaking divinely through his own body as through an instrument, we may know that it is as God that he does these things." So much from our blessed father Athanasius. Yet even though the body is called the Word's own, it is nevertheless from a woman and akin to ours, insofar as it is understood as flesh. And blessed Paul says: "The first man was of the earth, earthy; the second is from heaven." And Christ himself says: "No one has ascended into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man." We say that he speaks this way not because the Word brought down from heaven the body united to him; but since he himself was from above and from heaven, and made the body united to him his own, ineffably and inconceivably, without change and without confusion, for this reason he says that he is from heaven even when he had become Son of Man. Since, then, our argument is correct and blameless, what pretext is left to those who love to find fault for their ingenious charges against us, if the anathema fights against the blasphemies of certain people, setting the truth against falsehood? For my part, I think I have in no way fallen short of what is fitting in saying that Christ is above us. For even if the Word of God became man, yet even so he is… [Variant readings (?): "of those believing"; "which alone"; "puts into"; "persisting"; "and the"; "we have examined beforehand".]
…above not us alone but also all creation; for he is not understood only as man and like us, but the same one is also God from above and from heaven.

Anathema 12. If anyone does not confess that the Word of God suffered in the flesh, was crucified in the flesh, and tasted death in the flesh, and became firstborn from the dead, inasmuch as he is life and life-giving as God: let him be anathema.

Objection of the Orientals. Here again we remind him of his own words. For he calls the divine nature wholly impassible, speaking thus in his first tome: "One, then, who was worthier than all, laid down his own life for all; and by the economy he allows the flesh to be brought down to death for a little while; but he abolished death again as life, not enduring to suffer what is contrary to his own nature." Let us say to him, then, since he contradicts himself: How, then, does the one who allows the flesh to be brought down to death for a little while, and who abolishes death as life, not enduring to suffer what is contrary to his own nature, now, according to you, suffer through the flesh? No, God joined to the flesh did not suffer; rather, the flesh united to God the Word underwent what was proper to it, by his permission. For without his permitting it, no suffering or death would have come upon it. For if death does not come while the soul is present, how could suffering or death have troubled his own temple without his permission, when God was present—and not simply present, but joined to it by a supreme union comprehensible to him alone? No, it was not the Godhead joined to the flesh that suffered; rather, the flesh, with its permission, underwent what was proper to it. But that "he suffered in the flesh" is put by him with malicious intent, to mislead the simpler sort, is immediately evident; for he has not preserved impassibility for the divine nature. Whoever said "he suffered in the flesh" said nothing other than that he suffered with the flesh. If, then, he suffered with the flesh, he is confessed to be passible. For either he suffered because suffering belonged to his nature, or contrary to his nature. And if he suffered by nature, the Father too will be passible, since he is of one substance with the Son; for whatever belongs to the one begotten must surely belong to the one who begot him. Or else we confess that he suffered, being suited to suffering, but that the Father does not admit of suffering. But if we say this, we shall be agreeing with the heretics who say that the divinity of the only-begotten Son is passible, while that of the Father does not admit of suffering; which is why they also speak of a different substance. But if they say that he suffered contrary to nature, we shall reply: And what suffering is stronger than the divine nature, so as to drag the one who is by nature impassible into suffering contrary to nature? "His will," he says. But we say: his will [?]… We are looking for a suffering that [could have drawn] the impassible [nature]… [?] [Variant readings: "deception"; "suffering".]

…and transferred it into its own passibility. Besides, the divine will wills what befits it. "And what," he says, "is more fitting than to save the human race?" And how was the human race to be saved—by passing over itself into impassibility, or by dragging the divine and impassible nature down into suffering? For surely, as the stronger, it would have transferred the impassible into its own passibility. And what benefit is there for the passible if the impassible also becomes passible? The salvation of the passible is not the impassible's sharing with it through suffering; for that would rather increase the evil, not abolish it, since like is not abolished by like but increased. What, then, is the salvation of the passible? As we said, not the impassible's sharing with it, but its own transfer to impassibility. And this is what Christ the Lord did: he was not himself brought down into suffering in his divinity, but through his holy flesh he raised the whole of humanity on high, drew up to heaven what lay on the ground, and counted it worthy of the adoption as sons which it formerly had no boldness to claim. And who, after all, owed the death that came from disobedience? Human nature, surely, not the divine. Who, then, was it consistent should pay the death that came from disobedience?

Defense of Cyril. Truly admirable is the power of the truth, and experience is its witness. For I shall not need a long speech for my defense, that is, for persuading, as they suppose, those who have been deceived into thinking that we say the divine nature of the Word is passible, since our opponents, once they have come down to this point, have themselves quite plainly admitted that we stand clear of and outside the charges on these matters. But since, setting forth a groundless premise of their own devising, [unintentionally?] [?], and using bitter inventions of thought, they try to show off the force of the shrewdness within them, and argue very vigorously in declaring that the Word of God is impassible in his own nature, let them hear from us—since no one contradicts them—that they are boxing in vain and beating the air on this point, since no one holds the contrary. Why, then, do they sweat in vain and strain themselves needlessly? Who is so thunderstruck as to define the highest of all substances as passible, and to dare to cast down into the weakness of sufferings what is beyond everything begotten, and incorporeal? But since the doctrine of the mystery knows that the only-begotten, who is Son of God by nature, became man from a woman by the economy, and we affirm that the holy body taken from the blessed Virgin is his own, for this reason we say, quite correctly, that the sufferings of the flesh are called his by an appropriation belonging to the economy, while everywhere preserving… [Variant readings (?): "perhaps: or the [?]"; "as they suppose"; "having cast down"; "as strangers"; "stood"; "unwillingly"; "the Virgin Mary".]

…impassibility for his nature. For he is God from God. When, therefore, he is said to have suffered in the flesh, he is not understood to have suffered in his own nature, insofar as he is God, but rather as making the suffering his own; for the body united to him became his, as I said just now. For this reason the divine Paul also says that he himself, through whom and in whom the Father made all things, became firstborn from the dead. He writes thus: "Giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified us for a share in the inheritance of the saints in light, who has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption from sins. He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation; for in him all things were created, in the heavens and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities; all things were created through him and for him. And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together; and he is the head of the body, the Church. He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that in all things he might be preeminent. For in him it pleased all the fullness of the Godhead to dwell bodily, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven." Observe, then, how, after saying that all things were made through him, visible and invisible, thrones and authorities, he says that he was given to the Church as its head, and insists that he became firstborn from the dead, and that all things were reconciled through him to himself, and that he made peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven. Will anyone, then, still hesitate, and after this still needlessly fear that the doctrine of the mystery makes the Son's nature passible when he is said to have suffered in the flesh? For he makes his own, as I said, the sufferings of his own body. This was evidently the mind of the divine Peter when he says: "Since, then, Christ suffered for us in the flesh." It is one thing to be said to suffer in the flesh, and quite another to be said to suffer in the nature of the Godhead. For since the same one is at once God and man, impassible as regards the nature of the Godhead but passible as regards the human, what is absurd in saying that he suffered in that which is by nature capable of suffering, while remaining impassible in that which knows no suffering? And that the choir of the holy Fathers also shone with this same faith we shall learn from them, from what they themselves wrote, keeping the Savior's command; for they remembered his saying: "Freely you received, freely give." From Gregory, bishop of Nyssa: "Let this mind be in you," he says, "which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not [count equality with God a thing to be] seiz[ed]…" [Variant reading: "perhaps 'the one who hesitates'".]

[?] …did not count being equal with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant." What is poorer, for God, than the form of a servant? What is lowlier, for the King of the universe, than willingly to enter into partnership with our poor nature? The King of kings and Lord of lords puts on the form of a servant; the Judge of all becomes subject to the tribute of rulers; the Lord of creation takes lodging in a cave; he who holds the universe in his grasp finds no place in the inn, but is cast aside in a manger of dumb beasts; the pure and undefiled one accepts the filth of human nature, and, having passed through all our poverty, goes on as far as the experience of death. See the measure of his voluntary poverty: Life tastes death; the Judge is brought to judgment; the Lord of the life of all that exists is brought under the sentence of the one who judges; the King of every power above the world does not push away the hands of the executioners. "Let the measure of your humility," he says, "look to this example."

Of Basil, bishop of Caesarea. For heaven and earth, the vastness of the seas, the creatures that live in the waters and the animals of the dry land, plants and stars, air and seasons, and the varied ordering of the universe, do not demonstrate the surpassing greatness of his might so much as this: that God, who cannot be contained, was able, without suffering, to grapple with death through the flesh, so that by his own suffering he might grant us freedom from suffering.

Of Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria. And it was shown that he had the body not in appearance but in truth. It was fitting for the Lord, when he put on this human flesh, to put it on whole, together with its own passions, so that, just as we say the body is his own, so too the passions of the body might be called his alone, even though they did not touch him in his Godhead. If the body belonged to someone else, the passions too would be said to be that person's. But if the flesh is the Word's (for "the Word became flesh"), then the passions of the flesh must also be said to be his, whose the flesh is. For the one to whom the passions are attributed, chief among them being condemned, being scourged, thirsting, the cross, death, and the other [weaknesses] of the body [?]…

The passages set forth, then, are enough, I think, to give full assurance to those of sound mind, since the divine law expressly says, "At the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall be established." But if anyone still wishes to be contentious even after this, let him hear from us: "Go your own way." We, for our part, will follow [?] the true Scriptures and the faith of the holy Fathers, for in this way we shall win the prize of the upward calling in Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, forever. Amen.
